counterfactual.text: Spain, France, Switzerland and Austria's denial of overflight means that many US military aircraft involved in offensive operations in the Iran War or in resupply of the Israeli war effort must take a Northern European route. This has created a bottleneck that puts several Northern and Eastern European countries in stronger positions to disrupt the supply chain entirely - most notably Slovakia and Hungary could each break it completely through unilateral action. Other countries' impact is less certain but could still be decisive.

authorization_mechanism.text: Austria has no standing treaty or block clearance covering US military flights: the principal dispensation framework from single-flight clearance is the EDA Diplomatic Clearances programme (bilateral and multilateral agreements with certain countries also provide dispensation), whose participants are EU states plus Norway, so every US flight is individually vetted [3f2a9][b7e04]. Under § 8 Abs. 4 Luftfahrtgesetz (LFG), every entry into, exit from, and landing-free overflight of federal territory by a foreign military aircraft requires a permission of the Federal Minister of Defence, with the Foreign Minister heard before grant [8c41d]. Applications follow the BMLV clearance procedure published in AIP SUP 019/22, with applications filed on the published forms — the EU diplomatic clearance (DIC) form and a Dangerous Goods Details form [a3b80]; war-material transit additionally requires a separate Interior-Ministry authorization with a 40-working-day lead time [3f2a9]. Any presence of foreign troops, including air-force units merely crossing the border, is separately gated by the Truppenaufenthaltsgesetz [5efa2].

cooperation_2026.text: Cooperation during the 2026 Iran war was limited to flights unconnected to the belligerent operation, granted case-by-case within neutrality limits. On 2–3 April 2026 Austria approved the transit of a US EA-37B 'Compass Call II' electronic-warfare aircraft from the UK to Souda Bay, Crete — approved in coordination with the Foreign Ministry because Greece was not a party to the conflict, and subject to the strict condition that its reconnaissance sensors be switched off over Austrian territory, which was complied with [e35d0][946ab]. As regime context, the ministry stresses that it examines every application individually and approved over 5,000 foreign military overflights in 2025 alone [e35d0].

how_to_refuse.text: The Federal Minister of Defence can lawfully refuse any specific US flight, or all flights of a mission class, by withholding the § 8 Abs. 4 LFG permission, after hearing the Foreign Minister — no treaty renegotiation is required because per-flight permission is the statutory default [8c41d]. Mission-class refusal is documented practice: requests involving a country at war are refused, in coordination with the Foreign Ministry [1a6f8]. Two further independent gates exist: under § 2 Truppenaufenthaltsgesetz the Defence Minister, in agreement with the Foreign Minister, may grant any presence of foreign troops (including border crossing by air-force units), and must not permit it where troops carry war material impermissible under Austrian law [5efa2]; under § 3 Kriegsmaterialgesetz the Interior Minister, in agreement with the Foreign Minister (Defence Minister heard), may refuse war-material transit on any of six statutory grounds -- including international-law or foreign-policy conflict, transit into an area of armed conflict, and human-rights concerns, not solely the international-law/foreign-policy ground [c9037]. All are applied against the constitutional-rank Neutralitätsgesetz [d1905].

refusal_history.text: 2026 Iran war: the Defence Ministry confirmed on 2 April 2026 that US requests to use Austrian airspace had been refused from the outset — spokesperson Col. Michael Bauer: 'Es hat Anträge gegeben und diese wurden von Anfang an abgelehnt', adding that whenever a request involves a country at war it is refused — in this case in coordination with the Foreign Ministry [72cb1][1a6f8]. 2003 Iraq war: on 26 March 2003 the Nationalrat adopted a four-party resolution against the war, and Chancellor Schüssel declared neutral Austria would grant the belligerents 'keine Überflugsrechte' [2b8dc]. 1999 Kosovo: Austria denied overflight permits for NATO aircraft during Operation Allied Force [60e7f]. (On 10 May 2026 a US flyover request was on file for two US Air Force PC-12s routing RAF Mildenhall to Bucharest; Austria scrambled Eurofighters against a pair of PC-12s it said were flying without authorization, and around 2:10 p.m. two other USAF aircraft approached but turned away before entering Austrian airspace. On 11 May a newly submitted flyover request was approved and two PC-12s transited under Eurofighter monitoring. USEUCOM said the flight took place after 'an administrative error in the overflight clearance paperwork was corrected' [f48c3].)

counterfactual.text: US military flights between UK and German airspace whose shortest path would cross Belgium mostly route around it through the Netherlands; the exceptions are some shorthaul tactical airlift between UK and German bases. This concerns that traffic only, not the Gulf-bound flights the Foreign Minister described as transiting 'nos pays' (our countries).

authorization_mechanism.text: US military aircraft hold no automatic right to overfly Belgium: on the face of Belgian domestic law, overflight by foreign military aircraft is 'subordonné à l'autorisation du Ministre de la Défense nationale' (subject to the authorisation of the Minister of National Defence) under Belgian aviation law [a3f1c]. The Military AIP GEN 1.2 restates that approval rests with the Minister of Defence, with requests made through FPS Foreign Affairs, and offers annual standing diplomatic clearances with the broadest categories — dangerous cargo, arms and ammunitions, and overflight-and-landing of fighter and helicopter aircraft — reserved for EU and NATO members, a tier the United States is inside as a NATO member [e4b19]. The terms of those standing clearances depend on the applicable bilateral or multilateral agreement, and every flight not covered by one needs an occasional diplomatic clearance, requested on the EU Diplomatic Clearance (DIC) form at least five working days in advance [e4b19].

cooperation_2026.text: Belgium declined to restrict US aircraft involved in the 2026 Iran war. One Belgian overflight prohibition was in force from 22 January 2026 — the royal decree of 18 January 2026 — but it is keyed to military cargo bound for Israel or the occupied Palestinian territories, and does not reach Gulf-bound flights [0b41e]. On 1 April 2026 Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot told the Chamber commission that no prohibition reaching the aircraft involved in the war was envisaged, and gave the government's reason. In his words: 'il n'est pas envisagé à ce jour d'édicter une telle interdiction, car nous sommes conscients que nombre de ces avions militaires américains transitent par nos pays afin d'apporter l'aide militaire nécessaire aux pays du Golfe, pour qu'ils puissent légitimement se défendre contre les attaques iraniennes' (no such prohibition is envisaged as of now, because we are conscious that a number of these American military aircraft transit through our countries to bring the military aid the Gulf states need, so that they can legitimately defend themselves against Iranian attacks) [b5e82]. Spain, by contrast, announced it was closing its airspace to US aircraft involved in the war [2b9f4].

how_to_refuse.text: Two domestic routes could refuse overflight by a specific US flight or a whole mission class, neither requiring a change in Belgian legislation. Because authorisation is mandatory, the Minister of National Defence can withhold or condition it for a specific flight or class [a3f1c][e4b19]. The King may also bar a defined cargo, mission or destination class by royal decree, as with the royal decree of 18 January 2026, made under the aviation law's power to give effect to obligations arising from international treaties or from acts taken under them [c9e50][d2a86]. It reaches aircraft already holding the transport licences required for such cargo, obtained before the decree entered into force [d2a86]. Neither route singles out US nationality or the operator's belligerent status: the aviation law turns on foreign character generally [a3f1c], and the decree on what the cargo is and where it is going, reaching the recipient's belligerency rather than the carrier's [d2a86].

refusal_history.text:
Belgium enacted an overflight prohibition keyed to cargo and destination by royal decree of 18 January 2026, published and in force on 22 January [0b41e]. It rests on the King's power to give effect to international obligations, and its preamble invokes the three orders the International Court of Justice issued on 26 January, 28 March and 24 May 2024 directing Israel to meet its obligations under the Genocide Convention [d2a86]. Art. 2 bars overflight by aircraft carrying military materiel — the European Union's common military list under Common Position 2008/944/CFSP — that would strengthen 'de militaire capaciteiten van de aanwezige strijdende partijen' (the military capabilities of the belligerents present) and bound for 'de staat Israël of de bezette Palestijnse gebieden' (the State of Israel or the occupied Palestinian territories); art. 3 extends the bar to technical stopovers in near-identical terms [d2a86]. The decree defines overflight narrowly, as a flight by an aircraft 'dat is opgestegen vanuit een ander land' (that took off from another country) whose next stopover or final destination is a third country, so despite its title it does not reach cargo flown out of Belgium [d2a86].

No documented instance of Belgium refusing a US military overflight or landing request was located for the 1973 Yom Kippur airlift, the 1986 Libya raid, or the 2026 Iran war. For 1973 the accounts record a general refusal of overflight and refuelling by European allies [2fd60], and for 1986 France, Spain and Italy denying basing or overflight, in at least some cases [fc3f7]; neither names Belgium. For the 2003 Iraq war the record holds statements from two ministers. On 20 March 2003 Prime Minister Verhofstadt told the Chamber that the Foreign Minister had received a US pre-notification concerning overflights the previous evening and had informed him that he 'les a autorisés' (had authorised them) [4f7d3]. The same declaration was read to the Senate that afternoon [6a0b8]. Two weeks later, responding to a report of witness sightings of a B-52 over Belgian territory against an official routing that avoided Belgium, Defence Minister André Flahaut said 'Nous n'avons pas donné d'autorisation de survol et n'avons pas connaissance - par nos moyens - de tels survols' (we gave no overflight authorisation, and know of no such overflights by our own means) [9c4e1]. Belgium's other adopted measure is also directed at Israel, not the US: on 2 September 2025, in a decision on Palestinian sovereignty, the federal government instructed the Minister of Foreign Affairs 'to refuse, for as long as the war continues, requests from the Israeli authorities for military flights to overfly our airspace' [1a8e2].

counterfactual.text: Bulgaria is on the default and most common route. US military aircraft requiring resupply in Germany or the UK would need to reroute via Slovakia and Hungary to the Adriatic via Slovenia or Croatia, and from the Adriatic fly across the Mediterranean. This significantly lengthens the path. Bases in Romania would cease to be as useful.

authorization_mechanism.text: US Government aircraft and civil aircraft operating exclusively under US Department of Defense contract are authorized to overfly Bulgaria, conduct aerial refueling, and land and take off under Article IX(1) of the 2006 US-Bulgaria Defense Cooperation Agreement — a standing treaty authorization, exercised 'with full respect for the relevant rules of air safety and navigation,' whose operational details Article IX(3) leaves to an Implementing Arrangement [9b41e]. For US flights within its scope this treaty authorization displaces Bulgaria's default regime, under which the passage of allied or foreign armed forces is a transit crossing carried out only after permission from the competent state body (Art. 5(1) of the Act on the Crossing and Stay of Allied and Foreign Armed Forces) [3d7c2]. At the aviation layer, for flights by military aircraft the Minister of Foreign Affairs issues the flight permit only after the corresponding permission under that Act and coordination with the Minister of Defence (Regulation No. 22 of 22 Nov 2023, Art. 6(2)) [6f80a].

cooperation_2026.text: Bulgaria's Defense Cooperation Agreement framework with the United States remained in operation through 2026: US European Command stated that US forces operate at Bulgarian locations 'in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with allies and partners' [c25b9]. US refueling tankers were staging at Sofia airport under those arrangements until, in a move scoped to a visa dispute rather than a termination of the DCA, Bulgaria declined to extend their long stays and the tankers departed by 30 June 2026 [c25b9][82d4f]. The standing Article IX authorization for US Government and DoD-contract aircraft to overfly, refuel, land and take off was not withdrawn [9b41e]. On 22 July 2026 Bulgaria's parliament approved (136 votes to 13) the deployment of up to eight US KC-135 tanker aircraft and about 250 personnel at Bezmer air base from 24 July to 1 October 2026 [0333b].

how_to_refuse.text: Even for DCA-covered US flights, Bulgaria retains lawful levers short of treaty renegotiation. Under Article 9 of the Act on the Crossing and Stay of Allied and Foreign Armed Forces, the authority competent to issue a passage permission may terminate it 'if required by considerations of security and protection of national interests, in observance of international obligations' [1e6a8]. Permission for allied or foreign forces is allocated by mission character among the National Assembly, the Council of Ministers, and the Minister of Defence (Art. 10) [4b9d0], and operationally the Minister of Foreign Affairs can withhold the flight permit, or the Minister of Defence its coordination, under Regulation No. 22, Art. 6(2) [6f80a]. The Council of Ministers may additionally restrict air-navigation zones under Article 2(2) of the Civil Aviation Act [d3f57]. The June 2026 episode shows the head of government constraining US air presence through this executive chain without any treaty change [c25b9].

refusal_history.text: In late May-June 2026 Bulgaria's Prime Minister, Rumen Radev (formerly President, now head of government), declined to extend the presence of US military aircraft at Sofia airport, stating Bulgaria 'cannot respond positively to the request for long stays of aircraft and tankers at Sofia airport' and directing that US Air Force planes leave by the end of the month [c25b9][a7e13]. The stated basis was a visa/travel-waiver dispute rather than the DCA [c25b9]. All US military tanker aircraft had left Sofia airport by 30 June 2026 [82d4f].

counterfactual.text: Spain, France, Switzerland and Austria's denial of overflight means that many US military aircraft involved in offensive operations in the Iran War or in resupply of the Israeli war effort must take a Northern European route. This has created a bottleneck that puts several Northern and Eastern European countries in stronger positions to disrupt the supply chain entirely - most notably Slovakia and Hungary could each break it completely through unilateral action. Other countries' impact is less certain but could still be decisive.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military aircraft have no treaty right of overflight; access rests on Swiss domestic law. Under the Ordinance on the Safeguarding of Air Sovereignty (VWL, SR 748.111.1) Art. 4(1), foreign military and other state aircraft may overfly or land only with a permission (diplomatic clearance) [93418]. For routine flights the US holds a revocable annual authorisation (Jahresbewilligung), issued unilaterally by FOCA (BAZL) for clearly designated state aircraft, granted on the principle of reciprocity and withdrawable or amendable at any time when justified [8df7a][69e3f]. It excludes armed, combat and reconnaissance/electronic-warfare aircraft, landings, and troop, arms or war-material transports — each of which needs a single authorisation (Einzelbewilligung) stating the purpose of flight [8df7a]. FOCA grants clearances in consultation with the FDFA Directorate of International Law, the Military Aviation Authority, the Air Force and SECO, insofar as those bodies are concerned (VWL Art. 4(2)); politically significant requests go to the Federal Council [bc224].; requests of considerable political significance, in particular flights preparing or supporting combat operations, are decided by the Federal Council under Art. 4(4) [93418].

cooperation_2026.text: Switzerland kept access open for non-belligerent US flights within neutrality limits. In its 14 March 2026 decision the Federal Council approved three of the five US requests it considered: two transport-aircraft overflights for 15 March and one post-maintenance flight for 17 March, all judged unrelated to the conflict [5a723][65ff7]. It set a forward-looking rule that overflights demonstrably unrelated to the conflict, and humanitarian and medical transports including transport of the wounded, remain permissible, while requests exceeding the courant normal whose purpose cannot be established are rejected [5a723]. The US annual authorisation (Jahresbewilligung) for clearly designated state aircraft was maintained, excluding in particular state flights that would constitute military support in the war (the German original 'insbesondere' does not imply this is an exhaustive list of exclusions) [ab514]. FOCA continued clearing qualifying US flights case-by-case, approving 4 of 11 applications logged between 5 and 23 March [ccf85].

how_to_refuse.text: Refusal needs no treaty renegotiation, because every foreign military overflight already depends on a revocable Swiss permission. FOCA (BAZL) may refuse or condition any individual diplomatic clearance under VWL Art. 4(2) (SR 748.111.1), and the Air Force decides outside office hours under Art. 4(3) [792b2]. Requests of considerable political significance — expressly including flights serving the preparation or support of combat operations — are decided by the Federal Council under Art. 4(4) [792b2]. The US annual authorisation is itself an administrative act that 'may when justified be withdrawn or amended at any time' [87740]. Separately, LFG Art. 7 (SR 748.0) empowers the Federal Council to prohibit or restrict use of Swiss airspace on grounds of public order and security or for military reasons [c9b28]. Where the US is a belligerent, the law of neutrality (Hague Convention V of 1907, SR 0.515.21, applied mutatis mutandis to air war via customary law) obliges refusal of conflict-purpose military overflights [dfa3f].

refusal_history.text: Two episodes are documented, both overflight (no landing or basing — Switzerland hosts no US base). (1) Iraq war 2003: at the end of February 2003 the Federal Council decided to close Swiss airspace to military aircraft in the event of an attack without a UN mandate [4fed6]; when the operation was launched without explicit UN Security Council authorization on the night of 19-20 March 2003, the Federal Council treated it as a case for applying the law of neutrality, prohibiting overflight by aircraft participating in the conflict for military purposes — expressly including conflict-related reconnaissance and surveillance flights [c124d]; it lifted the measures on 16 April 2003 once hostilities had ceased [84d96]. (2) US-Israel-Iran war 2026: by 13 March FOCA had denied two US overflight requests on procedural grounds [9adca]; on 14 March the Federal Council, having classified the conflict as a war, rejected two of five US requests — two reconnaissance aircraft for 15 March — on neutrality-law grounds while approving three [5a723][65ff7]. FOCA rejected further requests case-by-case, approving only 4 of 11 US applications between 5 and 23 March [ccf85].

counterfactual.text: The Czech Republic is on the default and most common route for flights to and from the theater, whether transatlantic or connecting supply stops at German or UK bases. However, the possibility to reroute through Poland (if Poland would permit it) keeps the Czech Republic from being in the position of a single point of failure like Hungary or Slovakia each are. Additionally, there is reported broad support for the Iran War across multiple Czech political parties. Nonetheless, if the Czech Republic were to condition overflights, US operations could be substantially affected.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of the Czech Republic runs on a standing treaty authorization, not per-flight clearance. Article 11(2) of the 2023 Czech-US Defense Cooperation Agreement provides that aircraft operated by or exclusively for US forces 'shall be authorized to over-fly, conduct aerial refueling, land, and take off' within Czech territory, and Article 11(1) that they 'may enter, exit, and move freely' subject to 'respect for the relevant rules of air ... safety, security, and movement' [c1a90][4b6f2]. On a lex-specialis/later-in-time reading this standing authorization displaces, for US forces, the general Czech rule that 'no state aircraft may overfly ... the Czech Republic without permission,' under which other foreign military flights are cleared case-by-case by the Ministry of Defence's Department of Military Transport (NMCC CZE), typically at least 10 working days in advance [e83d5][7a2c8]. Constitutionally the Government is competent to decide on foreign-forces overflight (Art. 43(5)(a)) [9f0e1], while for US forces DCA Article 11(2) provides a standing treaty authorization for overflight [c1a90].

how_to_refuse.text: The Government of the Czech Republic decides on overflight of foreign armed forces under Constitution Art. 43(5)(a), a decision either chamber of Parliament may repeal by absolute majority under Art. 43(6) [9f0e1][2d5b7]. For US forces, whose overflight is granted standing authorization by DCA Art. 11(2), a blanket Government denial would conflict with the treaty. A generally-applicable airspace restriction is available: under §44 odst. 3 of the Civil Aviation Act (zákon 49/1997 Sb.) the Úřad pro civilní letectví, in agreement with the Ministry of Defence, may for the necessary time or permanently restrict or prohibit use of the airspace over defined areas on grounds of state defence or security [f6c34]. Whether such a closure lawfully binds a US Article 11 flight is a legal inference from the treaty's Art. 11(1) safety/security/movement proviso and §44(1)'s 'binding international treaty' clause; no located source states it [88785][4b6f2].

refusal_history.text: No refusal of US military overflight, landing or basing by the Czech Republic was located in the corpus. The 2023 Czech-US DCA was published as 39/2023 Sb. m. s. and entered into force on 22 September 2023 [d3923]; since then, US-forces aircraft overflight has rested on Article 11(2)'s standing treaty authorization [c1a90]. Parliament's power to repeal a Government overflight decision (Constitution Art. 43(6)) and the Government's own competence to decide on overflight (Art. 43(5)(a)) are the constitutional control mechanisms over foreign military flights [2d5b7][9f0e1]. This is a documented 'none found' in the searched sources, not proof that no conditioning ever occurred;

counterfactual.text: If Germany stopped permitting US military overflight or basing in connection with the Iran War, it would severely disrupt US logistics for the theater. Most resupply logistics for the relevant theater operate with steps in Ramstein, Spangdahlem, or UK bases. Prohibiting overflight would force a costly rerouting of all these supply routes, as even UK resupply would require wide rerouting through Poland. However, such a step is unlikely given the current German leadership under Chancellor Merz, lack of meaningful pushback by prior German governments in similar situations, concern over the US alliance and assistance to Ukraine, as well as Germany's "Staatsraeson" - the claim that Germany's fundamental purpose is to protect the Israeli state at all costs.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military aircraft hold no automatic, per-flight-free right to overfly Germany; the stationed US force's right to move in and over federal territory is expressly 'subject to the approval of the Federal Government' under Article 57(1)(a) of the Supplementary Agreement to the NATO SOFA, with only routine movements within German legal provisions (NATO-framework) deemed approved [393eb]. All foreign military aircraft entering (landing) or overflying Germany otherwise need a Military Diplomatic Clearance, issued as an annual standing clearance (Dauergenehmigung) or a single one/several-day clearance (Einzelgenehmigung) [b82da]. Applications are filed in good time through the German embassy and processed by the Federal Ministry of Defence, whose procedure is published in Military AIP GEN 1.2 [b82da][7d88e]. Entry permission is granted by the BMVg in agreement with the federal transport ministry under Sec. 30(2) LuftVG and Sec. 97(1) LuftVZO [b82da]. Movements outside the NATO framework remain fundamentally approval-requiring [94677].

cooperation_2026.text: Germany kept its territory and airspace open to US forces throughout the 2026 Iran war (which began in late February 2026), imposing no overflight or base restriction — the same contrary-grant posture visible in its refusal record [365ad]. Ramstein Air Base functioned as the relay and control hub for US Middle East operations, and Chancellor Merz permitted American forces to operate from German soil for the conflict [365ad]. Berlin publicly defended that access as lawful: government spokesman Stefan Kornelius called Ramstein's use 'in accordance with international law,' and Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said he saw 'no reason at present to doubt the legality' of the base's use while ruling out combat participation ('at most ... protection or material support') [365ad][9c3f1]. Iran's ambassador to Germany, Majid Nili, formally asked Germany in mid-March 2026 to 'clarify or explain' Ramstein's role, invoking UN General Assembly Resolution 3314, but the access was maintained [9c3f1].

how_to_refuse.text: The Federal Government, via the BMVg, can lawfully refuse specific US flights without treaty renegotiation: Article 57(1)(a) of the Supplementary Agreement to the NATO SOFA deems only routine NATO-framework movements approved, so movements outside that framework stay approval-requiring and refusable by mission classification [393eb][94677]; and the Military Diplomatic Clearance regime's single-flight Einzelgenehmigung, under Sec. 30(2) LuftVG and Sec. 97(1) LuftVZO, enables per-flight refusal [b82da]. The BVerwG held grave UN-Charter concerns existed against the 2003 Iraq war even as Germany's overflight and facility grants stood (2 WD 12.04, 21 Jun 2005) [a499c]; the Ramstein drone litigation found a protective duty only on a sufficient nexus plus serious danger of systematic international-law violation, leaving refusal to executive discretion below that threshold (BVerwG 6 C 7.19, 25 Nov 2020; BVerfG 2 BvR 508/21, 15 Jul 2025) [2abdb][5e2d3]. Contested commentary argues the Two-plus-Four 'only peace' clause with Basic Law Arts. 25/26 could oblige refusal of internationally unlawful missions, though this is not settled self-executing law [b2098].

refusal_history.text: The one documented instance of Germany restricting US military use of its territory or airspace was the October 1973 Yom Kippur War: after US resupply of Israel (Operation Nickel Grass) partly routed through and over West Germany and an Israeli ship loading arms at Bremerhaven became public, the Brandt government publicly prohibited resupply deliveries 'over or from' (über bzw. aus) German territory [bee7f][eb1e7]. Independent English-language scholarship corroborates that prohibition and the demand to halt deliveries [38864]. No refusal of a specific US overflight diplomatic clearance was located in the public record. The record instead shows contrary grants: in 2003 Germany opposed the Iraq war yet granted the US overflight rights and use of its installations in Germany [b867d].

counterfactual.text: Spain, France, Switzerland and Austria's denial of overflight means that many US military aircraft involved in offensive operations in the Iran War or in resupply of the Israeli war effort must take a Northern European route. This has created a bottleneck that puts several Northern and Eastern European countries in stronger positions to disrupt the supply chain entirely - most notably Slovakia and Hungary could each break it completely through unilateral action. Other countries' impact is less certain but could still be decisive.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of Spain runs on the bilateral Convenio de Cooperación para la Defensa (1988, amended 2002), whose authorizations are all subordinate to Spain's full sovereignty over its airspace (art. 24.1) [3142c]. Deployed US Forces aircraft — permanent or rotational, within the agreed force level — may overfly, enter and leave Spanish airspace with no requirement beyond Spanish air-traffic rules (art. 25.1), and aircraft based in Spain may fly between the bases listed in annex 2, which include Rota and Morón, on a filed flight plan [3142c]. Logistics-support flights operate under a quarterly blanket clearance granted by the Comité Permanente Hispano-Norteamericano (art. 25.2), which the 2011 operational procedure labels 'AUTORIZACIÓN GENERAL (BLANKET CLEARANCE)' [3142c][12a3c]. All other US aircraft need case-by-case authorization requested through the Comité's Spanish Section at least 48 hours ahead (art. 25.3) [3142c][0fd4c]. 'Special flights' — strategic bombers and combat or combat-support missions — require an individual request plus an explanatory memorandum, returned stamped AUTORIZADO or DENEGADO [0fd4c]. The AIP names the Ministry of Defence and the Foreign Ministry's overflight unit as clearance authorities [0a5a0].

cooperation_2026.text: Spain never suspended the bilateral Convenio or closed Rota and Morón during the 2026 Iran war; both operated normally until the ~2 March basing denial, and its refusals were scoped solely to Operation Furia Épica. Defence Minister Robles stated on 30 March 2026 that 'las bases están ahí' and that other actuaciones could still be carried out there, refusing only their use for the Iran war [6a07e]. Foreign Minister Albares likewise affirmed the installations remained 'bases de uso conjunto' — joint US-Spanish use under Spanish sovereignty — while withholding them for the offensive [09611]. Non-operation US use of the bases thus remained authorized under the standing arrangement, and the 30 March airspace closure expressly did not affect commercial traffic [84561]. This narrow scoping contrasts with June 2025, before the war, when the same government permitted US KC-135 tankers and bombers to stage from Rota and Morón for Operation Midnight Hammer against Iran [79834].

how_to_refuse.text: Denial of specific US flights requires no treaty renegotiation; the levers sit in instruments already in force [cfd26][a9081]. For any flight whose objectives exceed the Convenio's agreed defence scope, or in crisis situations, arts. 2.2 and 25.5 condition the flight on 'la autorización previa del Gobierno español', which the Government — acting through the Defence and Foreign ministries — can simply withhold [cfd26][f386e]. Within the treaty but outside the blanket categories, requests are processed by the Comité Permanente's Spanish Section, which obtains Air Force and Navy concurrence and returns each request stamped AUTORIZADO or DENEGADO [a9081]. Under general domestic law, transit of foreign state aircraft requires treaty cover or a special permit, so absent Convenio cover the Government may refuse a given flight (Ley 48/1960, art. 2) [497c0].

refusal_history.text: In April 1986 Felipe González's government refused both base use and overflight of Spanish airspace for the US raid on Libya (Operation El Dorado Canyon), forcing the F-111s to route around the Iberian Peninsula [04172]. On roughly 2 March 2026 the Sánchez government refused US use of the Rota and Morón bases for the offensive against Iran (Operation Furia Épica), withholding the prior authorization the Convenio conditions such uses on [88337]. On 25 March 2026 the Prime Minister told the Congreso that all flight plans contemplating Iran-operation actions had been rejected, expressly including refueling aircraft, and Spain then closed its airspace to any US military flight tied to the operation [d0aa3][0202f]. By contrast, nine months earlier, in June 2025, the same government had permitted US use of Rota and Morón for strikes on Iran (Operation Midnight Hammer, as named in The War Zone reporting) [62d7a].

This has created a bottleneck that puts several Northern and Eastern European countries in stronger positions to disrupt the supply chain entirely - most notably Slovakia and Hungary could each break it completely through unilateral action. Other countries' impact is less certain but could still be decisive.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of France rests on no automatic treaty right: Code des transports art. L6211-1 permits a foreign aircraft to circulate over French territory only under a diplomatic convention or an authorization [67992]. Instruction interministérielle n° 111 (annexed to the arrêté du 20 janvier 2017) provides that no foreign state aircraft may overfly or land without prior authorization, and makes the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs the office that examines and issues diplomatic overflight authorizations and notifies decisions of authorization, restriction or prohibition through diplomatic channels [66045]. Permanent authorizations with notification require prior notice of at least 24 working hours via diplomatic channel; they are granted, subject to reciprocity, for determined mission types, in principle per calendar year with automatic extension to 31 January pending renewal, and a separate notification-exempt permanent authorization covers EDA, EATC and NATO NRF flights (Instruction interministérielle n° 111) [a08b4].; occasional authorizations cover any mission not so covered [66045]. The EU/EDA arrangement creating annual blanket diplomatic clearances is open only to EU/Schengen states and cannot cover the US [4007e].

cooperation_2026.text: On 5 March 2026 France authorized US 'support' aircraft — refueling tankers and logistics transports, not combat aircraft — to land at the Istres and Avord air bases, on the condition stated by the French general staff that the assets concerned not participate in any way in the operations conducted by the United States in Iran [474a9]. Armed forces minister Catherine Vautrin, who said the authorization came from the President of the Republic and concerned refueling capacity only, put it: 'Un avion ravitailleur, c'est une station-service, ce n'est pas un avion de chasse' ('a refueling plane is a service station, it is not a fighter plane') [2186a]. On 31 March, the Élysée reportedly denied any overflight restriction, stating France 'has not changed position' since the beginning of the conflict, with landings limited to logistics transport aircraft at Istres and Avord.

how_to_refuse.text: Refusal requires no treaty step: the clearance regime is a unilateral French regulatory instrument resting on statute [d9dbb][67992]. Under Instruction interministérielle n° 111, the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs may refuse a diplomatic overflight authorization, notifying its decision through diplomatic channels, and may cancel or temporarily suspend an existing authorization or notification exemption — a lever reaching flights operating under a standing annual clearance [d9dbb]. Because occasional authorizations apply to any mission not covered by a permanent authorization, and permanent authorizations are limited to declared mission types, a specific US flight or an entire mission class can be denied at the clearance stage [d9dbb]. If a flight plan is filed without diplomatic authorization, the Ministry of Defence enforces the overflight prohibition after consulting the Prime Minister [d9dbb]. Separately, Code des transports art. L6211-4 allows overflight of designated zones to be prohibited for military or public-security reasons [06e94].

refusal_history.text: Around 28-30 March 2026 France denied Israel clearance to use French airspace for transporting American weapons destined for the war, reported by Reuters on 31 March, citing a Western diplomat and two informed sources, as the first such refusal since the Iran war began on 28 February [8f38d]. President Trump wrote that France 'wouldn't let planes headed to Israel, loaded up with military supplies, fly over French territory' [3a10f]. France denied any overflight restriction: a French military source told BFM TV that France 'has not restricted US military aircraft from flying over its airspace', with landing conditions unchanged — only logistical transport aircraft, at Istres and Avord [bf585]. As interpretation — France never confirmed the episode — the accounts reconcile as a discretionary single-flight clearance denial under the standing case-by-case regime, not a blanket closure [8f38d]. In April 1986 President Mitterrand refused overflight clearance for the US F-111 raid on Libya, forcing a detour around Iberia via Gibraltar; Spain likewise refused [d2c45][fc3f7].; this rests on consistent press and secondary accounts, not primary French records [c6bd3].

counterfactual.text: The UK is in the shortest flight path, and most flights to or from the European mainland fly over it. Some flights would route around the UK at greater length, but resupply at bases in the UK would not be feasible, substantially affecting US operations.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight works on two layers. For entry into UK airspace or landing, foreign state aircraft require Diplomatic Flight Clearance (DFC) under Chicago Convention Article 3, granted by the MOD Counter-Terrorism and UK Operations Directorate (CT&UKOps) [29804]. The US holds a standing dispensation: 'arrangements for a standing block approval [for State Aircraft] to land in the UK have been in place since at least 1949', per the Secretary of State for Transport [5d212]. Block-cleared states still file per-flight DFC for flights carrying Munitions of War, Forbidden Goods or VIPs landing in the UK, and for use of UK overseas military airfields; notice runs one week (UK airfields) to three weeks (RAF Akrotiri), clearance is valid 72 hours and flight details are confidential [29804]. Operational or combat use of UK bases, including 'combat operations by United States Air Force aircraft', is decided case-by-case under the 1952 Churchill-Truman 'joint decision' understanding [2b50d].

cooperation_2026.text: On 1 March 2026, reversing his February refusal, Prime Minister Starmer granted the US permission to conduct airstrikes on Iranian capabilities from British bases for 'a specific and limited defensive purpose' [6d16d][70023]. He framed the decision as 'the collective self-defence of longstanding friends and allies, and protecting British lives' [721ba], and told the Commons the UK would operate 'on a lawful basis' and would 'not join offensive action' [70023]. US B-52H and B-1B bombers subsequently deployed to RAF Fairford, with the approved scope reported to include striking Iranian missile sites before they could launch attacks [00dca].

how_to_refuse.text: Three refusal levers exist without treaty change. MOD CT&UKOps can refuse Diplomatic Flight Clearance per flight — 'requests may be turned down' and 'No guarantee of clearance can be assumed' [2f214] — and the US standing block approval leaves flights carrying Munitions of War or Forbidden Goods, VIP landings, and use of UK overseas military airfields subject to per-flight DFC [2f214][339a5]. The Secretary of State for Transport can withhold the separate authorisation required for Forbidden Goods [2f214]. For operational or combat use of UK bases, HM Government decides case-by-case under the Churchill-Truman 'joint decision' understanding, engaged in the 1973, 1998 and 2026 refusals above [2b50d]. Heath told the Commons that 'not only is there a right of veto, but that it has been used and accepted by the United States' [3a700], though declassified files record that whether Britain holds a genuine veto over US base use 'has never been fully resolved' [7f3af].

refusal_history.text: During the October 1973 Yom Kippur War the Heath government refused to allow the US to resupply Israel from British bases, ruling out those in Cyprus, and restricted US reconnaissance flights from UK installations [f9096].; Heath told the Commons in 1986 that 'The reply which my Government sent to the United States was no' [f4c22]. In 1998 ministers refused two US rendition requests: the Foreign and Defence Secretaries refused use of RAF Akrotiri to refuel a flight carrying two Hizballah members, and an October request to refuel at Prestwick an aircraft carrying a detainee to Egypt was, on officials' recollection, also refused [e273d]. In February 2026 Prime Minister Starmer initially denied a US request to stage strikes on Iran from RAF Fairford and Diego Garcia, reportedly on advice that support could breach international law [ea83a][7adbd]. The contrasting April 1986 Libya grant was itself conditioned: Thatcher 'reserved the position of the United Kingdom on any question of further action which might be more general' [d3af5].

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of Greece runs on per-flight diplomatic clearance, not a standing treaty right: the Air Code (Law 1815/1988), Article 2, asserts 'full and exclusive sovereignty over Greek airspace' and permits foreign aircraft to circulate only under the Code, special laws, international conventions, or special permits, and the Hellenic National Defence General Staff officially defines entry 'without permission (diplomatic clearance)' as a violation of national airspace [3f09d][e1815]. Clearance requests are handled by the Hellenic Air Force General Staff, International Relations Office, Section of Diplomatic Clearances and Overflights, Greece's national Office of Primary Responsibility [b52e8]. The principal bilateral instrument, the 1990 Mutual Defense Cooperation Agreement as amended in 2019 and 2021 (ratified by Law 4932/2022), grants US forces access to named installations, with 'priority status (unimpeded access and use)' at designated non-military infrastructure — the Port of Alexandroupolis and other locations as mutually agreed — a facilities/base-access framework [91d4a][c6e72][5ab90].

cooperation_2026.text: Greece imposed no airspace closure or clearance restriction on US forces during the 2026 Iran war and appears in no list of European states denying US access for Iran-linked operations [d971e]. Souda Bay continued as a US logistics and carrier hub — the USS Gerald R. Ford docked there on 23 February 2026 — and Greece deployed an anti-missile battery on Karpathos to protect the base after Iran's IRGC named Souda a legitimate target [d971e][64c0a]. Foreign Minister Gerapetritis reportedly characterized Souda's role as mainly logistical and 'unsuitable' for offensive operations, with US operations 'strictly governed by a pre-existing bilateral agreement' [64c0a]. Greece declined only the separate Hormuz naval-escort mission [64c0a].

how_to_refuse.text: Entry of a foreign aircraft into Greek airspace without permission (diplomatic clearance) is officially defined by the Hellenic National Defence General Staff as a violation of national airspace [3f09d]; the Air Code (Law 1815/1988) Article 2 asserts the Greek state's full and exclusive sovereignty over Greek airspace [e1815]. The regime is natively per-aircraft/per-mission: each foreign state aircraft needs its own clearance from the Hellenic Air Force General Staff's Section of Diplomatic Clearances and Overflights, so refusal of an individual flight is the ordinary operation of the system [b52e8]. At the political level, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of National Defence are Greece's designated representatives under the MDCA, through whom locations and activities are mutually agreed [91d4a]. Refusal grounds beyond the individual flight — mission class, purpose, destination, or a blanket bar on all US flights — are inferences from the general sovereignty regime rather than codified levers.

refusal_history.text: The 1973 Yom Kippur War episode is contested in the scholarship. As related by Kallivretakis (2014), the junta's foreign minister Xanthopoulos-Palamas declared on 13 October 1973 that Greece's friendly relations with the Arab states 'precludes participation, either directly or indirectly, in any actions that might be directed against them', asserting that Greece was not being used in connection with the Middle East situation [7d3c5][55b22]; the secondary literature contains contradictory accounts of whether the junta quietly facilitated or resisted US resupply operations, and this claim requires further primary-source research before it can be stated definitively [7d3c5]. According to Markezinis's memoirs as presented by Kallivretakis, on 21 November 1973 Washington requested expanded port facilities and use of the Elefsina airport for the landing of aircraft 'with nuclear arms [...] outside of NATO planning'; Markezinis recommended rejection the next day and Papadopoulos agreed 'without reservation' (pp. 115-116) [55b22]. In 1974-75 the Karamanlis government withdrew base access after the Cyprus crisis (Elefsis home-porting ended; Hellenikon airbase closed) while permitting US landings for Greek defense needs — base-access withdrawals, not overflight bans [f42b6]. By contrast, in 2003 Greece issued what Brady Kiesling, writing in the New York Review of Books, described as 'blanket flight clearances' and Souda handled thousands of US military flights [08e9d]; this research located no modern refusal of a specific US overflight or landing clearance.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of Croatia runs through a two-key diplomatic-clearance regime, not a standing treaty right. Under the Air Traffic Act (Zakon o zračnom prometu) čl. 15(3)(1), approval of foreign military aircraft is issued by the Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs (MVEP) 'uz suglasnost ministarstva nadležnog za poslove obrane' (with the consent of the Ministry of Defence), so either ministry can withhold it [aa11b]. Applications are filed by the sending state's diplomatic mission [bb22c]; Pravilnik NN 50/2017 sets a single clearance at five working days (seven for dangerous goods) plus purpose-limited annual clearances [bb22c][ee55f]. NATO Response Force lanes are expedited (annual ≥15 working days; single combat/refuelling ≥3 working days; crisis ≥2 days) [dd44e]. No located US-Croatia treaty displaces this regime: the 2004 training MOU (TIAS 06-111) carries only a training-scoped charges exemption, the 2008 SOFA governs status of forces, and TIAS 17-724 is the unrelated CUV-ME unmanned-vehicles R&D agreement [11a7b][22b8c][ff66a].

cooperation_2026.text: Croatia imposed no restriction on US military access during the 2026 war and affirmatively hosted US assets. The USS Gerald R. Ford, which had been conducting strike operations against Iran, made a port call at Split on 28 March 2026 with no reported Croatian objection [55e1f]. Glas Istre reported on 1 July 2026 that a US military KC-135 had been seen at Pula Airport, the airport stating that such flights take place 'in accordance with valid international regulations and approvals from the competent national bodies' [da314] — i.e. Croatian national clearance had issued [66f2a]. On 27 May 2026, amid a Slovenia-Israir landing-permit dispute in which Slovenia's infrastructure ministry revoked Israir's seasonal permit, an Israir-branded flight landed in Zagreb rather than Ljubljana; Israir said Slovenia had refused the landing and diverted the flight mid-route, which Slovenia's Ministry of Infrastructure disputed, saying the flight had been filed for Zagreb before departure [77a3b]. Croatia appears in none of the 2026 roundups of European states restricting US/Israeli military access [88b4c].

how_to_refuse.text: Croatia could refuse a specific US flight without treaty renegotiation: foreign military flights require diplomatic clearance under the Pravilnik regime [bb22c], and the 2017 US-Croatia unmanned-maritime-vehicles cooperation agreement (a bilateral defence agreement) contains no standing overflight right that would displace it [ff66a]. MVEP, which issues diplomatic clearances, can decline one — and because Air Traffic Act čl. 15(3)(1) conditions military-aircraft approval on Ministry of Defence consent, either ministry can block a flight [aa11b]. Pravilnik NN 50/2017 čl. 17(1) supplies the operative refusal grounds, including threat to national security, absence of the required defence-ministry consent, and breach of internationally assumed obligations, and any single clearance 'neće se izdati' (shall not be issued) on these [cc33d]. A categorical airspace ban is machinery Croatia has used — in February 2022 it prohibited Russian-operated aircraft from entering or overflying Croatian airspace by NOTAM [44d0e] — while entry of allied armed forces into Croatia requires a decision of the Croatian Parliament proposed by the Government with the President's prior consent, with exceptions for exercises and training approvable by the Government with the President's consent (Ustav čl. 7) [33c9d].

refusal_history.text: This research located no documented Croatian refusal of a US or allied military overflight, landing, or basing in any era, across the 1990s war period, the 2003 Iraq war, and the 2026 Iran war. In 1994-95, under UN Security Council Resolution 958 — which extended the NATO air-power authorization to Croatian airspace subject to close coordination with the Secretary-General and UNPROFOR — NATO struck the Serb-held Udbina airfield on 21 November 1994 at UNPROFOR's request; that airspace was then under Serb/RSK rather than Zagreb-government control, and Croatia (a NATO member only from 2009) did not refuse the operation [99c5d]. The North Atlantic Council's decision of 24 November 1994 on using air power against aircraft in Croatian airspace was taken 'subject to making arrangements with the Croatian authorities' [d6898].; that airspace was then under Serb/RSK rather than Zagreb-government control, and Croatia (a NATO member only from 2009) did not refuse the operation [99c5d]. The North Atlantic Council's decision of 24 November 1994 on using air power against aircraft in Croatian airspace was taken 'subject to making arrangements with the Croatian authorities' [d6898]. Croatia operates a standing clearance regime for allied military flights: Pravilnik NN 50/2017 Article 19 provides NATO Response Force flights diplomatic clearances — annual, individual, or general — issued by the foreign ministry with defence-ministry consent [dd44e].

counterfactual.text: Blocking Hungarian airspace would severely complicate US logistics and force costly rerouting for the relevant theater. Hungary and Slovakia are in the unique position of a single point of failure: each individually connects the no-fly zone across Spain, France, Switzerland and Austria in the west. After long rule by Viktor Orban's Fidesz party, PM Peter Magyar and his Tisza party were recently elected in a landslide - promising reintegration with the EU and NATO. Foreign policy intent is not yet fully known, but it seems unlikely that on this platform Hungary would alienate the US, unless it had wide European backing. Blocking Hungarian airspace would block all US flights to or from the theater using British or German resupply stations, as well as direct arcs between the United States and the Middle East. Flights would need to pass without resupply across the Mediterranean south of Spain. The throughput of the US' Mediterranean bases for this volume is unverified. If the Hungarian government looked likely to deny overflight, it is most likely that without wider European backing, the US would threaten them or offer concessions. However, this does put the Hungarian government in a position of extraordinary leverage.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of Hungary is authorized by standing arrangement, not per-flight clearance. Article XI(2) of the 2019 US-Hungary Defense Cooperation Agreement (promulgated as Act LI of 2019, in force 21 August 2019) authorizes aircraft operated by or exclusively for US forces to over-fly, conduct aerial refuelling, land and take off within Hungarian territory, subject only to 'the relevant rules of air safety and navigation' [f4a21]. This is reinforced domestically: section 7(3) of the Aviation Act (Act XCVII of 1995) exempts NATO- and EU-member-state state aircraft from the entry-permission requirement applied to other foreign state aircraft [6c9d8], and AIP Hungary GEN 1.2 confirms such aircraft 'may operate based on the submitted Flight Plan' [b3e07]. No office issues a routine per-flight approval and no advance mission disclosure is required; only US transport of arms, heavy equipment and hazardous materials triggers a duty for the competent authorities to 'cooperate regarding procedures' under DCA Article XI(5) [92f16].

how_to_refuse.text: Hungary retains one clear, treaty-compatible lever, though its use to bar a specific US flight is inferential. Because the DCA grants standing overflight/landing rights and Aviation Act section 7(3) exempts NATO state aircraft, the ordinary diplomatic-clearance gate cannot reach routine US flights; the weapons/dangerous-goods single-entry-clearance requirement also does not apply to them, since Government Decree 4/1998 section 3(3) expressly limits that requirement to foreign state aircraft NOT covered by the section 7(3) exemption [a7c40]. During a state of national crisis or state of emergency declared under the Fundamental Law (the cases of Decree 4/1998 §7(1)), use of the relevant airspace may be restricted in time and space to ensure airspace sovereignty, per the National Defence Act's traffic-restriction provisions, with the aviation authority notifying those affected (§8(1), §8(3)) [5d8b3]. No source describes Hungary denying an actual US flight, so applying this restriction power to a specific US mission is an inference from the combined treaty and airspace texts, not a directly stated rule.

refusal_history.text: The legal posture points away from refusals: the DCA grants US-forces aircraft standing authorization and domestic law exempts NATO state aircraft from diplomatic clearance, so routine US flights are neither individually approved nor individually denied [f4a21][6c9d8]. This is a documented 'none found' within the searched sources rather than an assurance that no conditioning has ever occurred; under DCA Article XI(5), the competent authorities of the Parties 'shall cooperate regarding procedures for U.S. transportation of arms, heavy equipment, and hazardous materials' within Hungary [92f16].

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of Ireland runs on a standing arrangement dating from 1959: qualifying overflights that are unarmed, carry only cargo and passengers, and comply with navigational requirements are permitted without prior notification, a 'blanket clearance' [eb8f0][db9d9]. That arrangement is a policy arrangement dating from 1959, resting on the discretionary permission power in the Air Navigation (Foreign Military Aircraft) Order 1952 [eb8f0][cef50]. Any flight outside those criteria, including every landing and any armed, operational or intelligence overflight, needs advance express permission of the Minister for Foreign Affairs under article 3 of that Order [cef50][eb8f0]. Requests are routinely required to confirm the aircraft is unarmed, carries no arms, ammunition or explosives, will not gather intelligence, and is not part of a military exercise or operation [eb8f0]. The US Embassy submits post-facto overflight notifications to the Department of Foreign Affairs on a monthly basis [eb8f0].

cooperation_2026.text: Ireland kept US military access open throughout the 2026 Iran war. The Irish Times Investigations Unit found that over the fifteen months to April 2026 the Government refused no US military overflight or landing request, and US military overflights surged 56% from February to March 2026 [51bef]. Two USAF C-130H Hercules transited Shannon around 28 February-1 March 2026, arriving from Canada [4a610][13989], reported by The Ditch to be onward to the Ramstein weapons hub used against Iran [4a610]. Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee declined to close Irish airspace as Spain and Switzerland had, saying there was 'no reason to believe' US aircraft in the Iran war were overflying Ireland [51bef]. Immediately before the war, Ireland granted the October 2025 exemption and diplomatic clearance for a US-chartered Omni Air flight to refuel at Shannon carrying munitions to Israel's Nevatim base — its first acknowledged Israel-bound weapons authorisation since 2006 [d0471][d2fcc].

how_to_refuse.text: Two discretionary domestic instruments let Ireland refuse specific US flights today without renegotiating any treaty. For military or state aircraft, the Minister for Foreign Affairs may refuse express permission for any landing, or any overflight falling outside the 1959 blanket, under article 3 of the Air Navigation (Foreign Military Aircraft) Order 1952, and may attach stipulations under article 4 [cef50][df836]. For civil aircraft, carriage of munitions of war is prohibited unless the Minister for Transport by direction exempts the class of aircraft under article 5 of the Air Navigation (Carriage of Munitions of War, Weapons and Dangerous Goods) Order 1973 [d152b]; documented refusal grounds include the nature of the munitions carried and where the flight was due to travel to or from [b968c]. Both powers operate flight-by-flight. Whether the 1959 blanket could lawfully be revoked wholesale for all US military overflights is inferential, not settled law.

refusal_history.text: No refusal of a US military overflight or landing has been located in any era: the Department of Foreign Affairs confirms no US military aircraft was prevented from landing in 2022-2024, and the Irish Times found none was refused in the 15 months to April 2026 [9e484][3d5e9]. Ireland's only exercised refusals are civil-charter munitions-exemption denials by the Minister for Transport, distinct from the never-refused military track: nineteen civil aircraft were refused in 2014 over indiscriminate-munitions concerns [1abec]; an Omni Air charter was refused landing at Shannon on 21 May 2022 [02f96]; and two Omni Air flights were refused overflight on 8 and 30 July 2024 'based on the nature of the total munitions of war proposed to be carried' [9e484]. Even in wartime Ireland declined to refuse: in March 2003 the Dail voted 77-60 to continue US overflight and landing rights during the Iraq war [86067].

counterfactual.text: Italy has not denied all overflight, but it did signal refusal of staging - as is their prerogative under treaty - through at least one denial. Nevertheless, the Sigonella base on Sicily remains one of the US military's most used European staging points during the current war. Italy's denial is not decisive in the presence of the more comprehensive overflight restrictions by Spain, France, Switzerland and Austria, but would increase in importance if any of those countries' policies were to change.

authorization_mechanism.text: Foreign military aircraft, US aircraft included, may not overfly Italian territory without a 'speciale autorizzazione' of the Ministry of Defence under article 794, paragraph 2, of the Codice della navigazione [4be27]. Above this statutory per-flight rule sits the bilateral base/airspace framework of the classified 1954 Bilateral Infrastructure Agreement as implemented by the 1995 'Shell' memorandum of understanding; Italian institutional practice under it, recorded in the 21 January 2003 joint parliamentary committee record, is that the grant of an overflight or base-use request 'is not automatic' and authorization 'can be denied by the Government' in cases of particular political salience, and the 2006 Sigonella Technical Arrangement requires any use of the bases to be coordinated beforehand with the responsible national military authority [7f30a]. Reporting on the agreements describes a two-tier practice: routine activities such as in-flight refuelling and logistical support proceed automatically under the agreements, while acts of war require formal government approval [c25e8]. Requests are examined carefully, case by case [e6b72].

cooperation_2026.text: Alongside its kinetic refusals, Italy cooperated substantially with US non-kinetic operations throughout the 2026 Iran war: by Defence Minister Crosetto's own count, 518 flights departed from US bases in Italy between 28 February and 23 June 2026 [5cd09]. Crosetto stated on 31 March 2026 that the bases were 'attive, in uso e nulla è cambiato' (active, in use, and nothing has changed), with the Government acting in full adherence to commitments made in Parliament [68a1f]. On 24 June 2026, rebutting NATO Secretary-General Rutte's claim that 500 US aircraft had taken off from Italy to support the operation, Crosetto stated that 'Italy authorizes exclusively the flights foreseen by the treaties, which totally exclude kinetic activities' — as Italy 'has always done and will continue to do under the current agreements' — and that whenever a request outside that perimeter arose, Italy did not grant authorization [b04e3].

how_to_refuse.text: The Ministry of Defence can lawfully refuse specific US military flights, or all flights of a mission class, simply by withholding the 'speciale autorizzazione' required by article 794, paragraph 2, of the Codice della navigazione — a per-flight domestic-law power needing no treaty renegotiation [4be27]. For missions launched from or supported by US-used bases, the 2006 Sigonella Technical Arrangement requires prior coordination with the responsible national military authority, and per the Government's 2003 statement to Parliament authorization 'can be denied by the Government' in cases of particular political salience [7f30a]; it is the Italian government that decides whether to authorize operations from bases in Italy directed abroad [c25e8]. As a backstop, under article 793 ENAC may, at the request of the competent administration, prohibit overflight of specified zones for military, security or public-order reasons, and the Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport may prohibit air navigation over the entire national territory for exceptional reasons of public interest [d91c4].

refusal_history.text: On 14-15 April 1986, the Craxi government refused the United States use of Italian airspace for the raid on Libya (Operation El Dorado Canyon), forcing the F-111s onto a roughly 1,300-mile-longer route via Gibraltar [2e85c]. On 19 March 2003, for the Iraq war, the government granted airspace overflight and base use for transit, refuelling and maintenance but expressly excluded making military facilities available as bases for direct attack on Iraqi objectives [f473d]. On Friday 27 March 2026, Defence Minister Guido Crosetto denied US aircraft landing/use of the Sigonella naval air station en route to kinetic operations against Iran, because the authorization request was submitted only after the aircraft were already airborne [3a9d1][91f4b][e6b72]. Crosetto later confirmed this was not isolated: Italy refused 'several of those flights, not just one' [5cd09].

authorization_mechanism.text: Ordinary civil overflight of Kuwait is free, but any flight 'involved in diplomatic or military operations' must apply in advance to the civil-aviation authority, and non-traffic (refuelling/crew-rest) stops require a minimum notice period of 48 hours [33861]. The nature of the flight must be disclosed—for example, transport of ammunition [33861]. This regime rests on the primary air-navigation statute, under which an aircraft not registered in Kuwait 'shall not fly over or land in the [territories] of Kuwait except under an authorisation granted by His Highness the Emir' [ee632], operational permission being granted by the Kuwait Civil Air Administration on the Emir's behalf [33861][44675]. The clearing office named in the published procedure is the Directorate General of Civil Aviation [33861].

cooperation_2026.text: The US installations it hosts, notably Ali Al Salem Air Base and Camp Arifjan, were struck by Iranian missiles and drones during the conflict [b5a6e][6935d]. Kuwait hosted roughly 13,500 US personnel at the time of the strikes [6935d]. Kuwaiti forces acted as host-nation defender, intercepting Iranian missiles and drones aimed at these sites, while the Emir ordered heightened protection of vital national facilities and affirmed Kuwait 'had not authorized military operations from its territory' [b5a6e][1b78a]. The parallel OKAC/Kuwait FIR closure applied only to civil overflight/transit—arrivals and departures at Kuwait International remained permitted with prior DGCA approval—and did not suspend the US bases [d95b5].

how_to_refuse.text: Two levers are clear law. Administratively, any flight 'involved in diplomatic or military operations' must apply to the civil-aviation authority—named in the published procedure as the Directorate General of Civil Aviation—which can therefore withhold clearance [ea6bd]. Under Kuwait's air navigation law, a non-Kuwaiti aircraft 'shall not fly over or land in the territories of Kuwait except under an authorisation granted by His Highness the Emir' — overflight and landing consent is thus the Emir's to grant or refuse [fea95]. For an actual US military mission, that refusal is exercised as sovereign executive discretion at head-of-state/cabinet level, as when Kuwait refused any use of its territory against Iran in 2026 [e22e4]. The precise internal organ (Emir, Council of Ministers, or Ministry of Defence) that would deny a specific foreign military mission is not established from a retrievable primary text.

refusal_history.text: On 9 March 2026, during the war in which Iran struck Kuwaiti sites, the Emir Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah stated in a televised address that Kuwait 'did not permit the use of our land, our airspace, or our coasts/waters for any military action against' Iran [73516][784f3][1958c]. Because Kuwait hosts major US installations, this barred any use of its territory, airspace or bases—including by US forces—for strikes on Iran, as a standing mission-class posture rather than the denial of one identified flight [73516]. No episode of Kuwait refusing a single, specifically identified US military overflight or landing was located in the public record [73516].

counterfactual.text: Most transatlantic flights cross Dutch airspace. It is notable that almost all flights that are not shorthaul tactical airlift which would fly over Belgium as the shortest path, route around it through the Netherlands instead. There is also a common air refuelling circuit near Eindhoven in the southeast, where the NATO Multinational MRTT tanker fleet is based. While flights between UK airspace (or the North Atlantic) and German airspace would become substantially longer if the Netherlands stopped permitting US military overflight, it would still be possible to bypass and enter German airspace directly from the North Sea or the same in the opposite direction.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military aircraft overfly the Netherlands not under a bilateral treaty but under a unilateral, revocable domestic instrument: the NAVO-binnenvliegregeling of 8 September 1987, whose art. 1(1) permits military aircraft of NATO-affiliated states to enter Dutch airspace and use the listed military airfields [794e8]. The cabinet confirms that US military aircraft use Dutch airspace on the basis of this regulation 'and supplementary diplomatic clearances' [0c5ab]. The baseline regime beneath it is the 1959 Besluit toelating vreemde militaire luchtvaartuigen: entry only after a permit requested through diplomatic channels, disclosing the flight's purpose, aircraft, occupants, route, landing places and timing [3850f]. Flights deviating from the regulation's conditions require a request to the Minister of Defence six working days in advance [3a962]; ECM flights and weapons/munitions carriage need special ministerial permission [c2e48]. The deciding office throughout is the Minister of Defence, under a delegation from Luchtvaartwet art. 76(1)(d) [3850f][d6a5c].

cooperation_2026.text: The Netherlands expressly kept its airspace and bases open to US military flights during the 2026 Iran war. Answering parliamentary questions from member Dassen (Volt) — prompted by Spain's closure of its airspace to conflict-related military aircraft — the cabinet stated on 4 May 2026: 'Het kabinet is niet voornemens om het Nederlandse luchtruim of militaire bases te sluiten voor militaire of commerciële vracht' (the cabinet does not intend to close Dutch airspace or military bases to military or commercial cargo) [2d89e][bac4b]. It reaffirmed that US military aircraft may use Dutch airspace on the basis of the NAVO-binnenvliegregeling and supplementary diplomatic clearances, and declined for operational reasons to comment on individual military flight movements [2d89e][e0c68].

how_to_refuse.text: The Minister of Defence can lawfully refuse specific US flights or a mission class today without touching any treaty, because the operative instruments are domestic. Under NAVO-binnenvliegregeling art. 1(2) the Minister may withdraw, amend or condition the standing NATO clearance 'al dan niet voor een bepaald geval' (whether or not for a particular case) — reaching a single flight, a category of flights, or the clearance wholesale, reverting US aircraft to the 1959 Besluit art. 2 case-by-case permit regime [d7c0b][17ef4]. ECM flights and carriage of weapons, munitions or bombs are carved out of the standing clearance and need special ministerial permission, so those mission classes can be refused case by case [0de23][65132]. Under Besluit art. 5(2) the Minister may order a foreign military aircraft within Dutch jurisdiction to leave by a designated route, by force if necessary [17ef4]. The enabling delegation, Luchtvaartwet art. 76(1)(d), remains in force [d6a5c].

refusal_history.text: No instance was located, in any era, of the Netherlands refusing US military overflight, landing or basing [d943e][56d34]. The illuminating contrary datum is October 1973: unlike several NATO allies that year, Defence Minister Henk Vredeling permitted an American military airlift via Schiphol and authorised secret Dutch deliveries of munitions and spare parts to Israel, for which the Netherlands was placed under the OAPEC oil embargo (October 1973 - March 1974). [d943e][56d34][88f5a].

counterfactual.text: Almost no US military flights for this war transit Polish airspace. Poland is a major hub for military aid to Ukraine, a separate track from this conflict. Geographically Poland can substitute for the Czech Republic: both border Germany and Slovakia, so either can serve as the approach leg, though routing via Poland lengthens the path. It cannot substitute for Slovakia or Hungary — from Poland the only onward path south is Slovakia, since Ukraine and Belarus carry no traffic at all. Polish denial would therefore displace the approach, not close the corridor.

authorization_mechanism.text: For US forces, overflight of Poland rests on a standing treaty authorization rather than a per-flight diplomatic request: under the 2020 US-Poland Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA, TIAS 20-1113), art. 13(1), aircraft operated by or exclusively for US forces 'shall be authorized to over-fly, conduct aerial refueling, land, and take off within the territory of Republic of Poland,' exempt from air-navigation, landing and parking fees — though exercised 'in accordance with mutually determined procedures' and a flight-designation 'implementing arrangement' [4d1a2]. The domestic default for other foreign military aircraft is per-mission: under the Act of 12 October 1990 on the protection of the state border, art. 18a(1), a flight requires a permission (zezwolenie) issued by the Operational Commander of the Branches of the Armed Forces [5e2b3]. Prawo lotnicze art. 150 routes all foreign state aircraft to that Border Act regime and to binding international agreements [7a4d5]. Whether that standing authorization extends to flights supporting operations against a third state is not addressed anywhere in the treaty's Polish ratification record [5b8c4]; see "Legal: How to say no".

cooperation_2026.text:
Poland imposed no restriction on US military overflight, landing or basing during the 2026 war, and no such restriction appears in any survey of European states that limited US access [0d7a8][8b5e6]. It nonetheless declined to participate. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said on 3 March that "No such request has been made [8562a]. Poland is not participating in this operation" [c5d19]. On 12 March, asked whether the US could use bases in Poland against Iran, Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski answered "Nie mamy takich baz" ("We don't have such bases"), adding that President Karol Nawrocki had already stated he would not consent to "udział wojska polskiego w tej wojnie" ("Polish military participation in this war") [a7c31]. Sikorski separately ruled out the Redzikowo Aegis Ashore site being used against Iran, on the ground that its governing agreements scope it to missiles threatening Europe or the United States and "Takich rakiet Iran nie wystrzelił" ("Iran did not fire such missiles") [a7c31][b2f48]. Prime Minister Donald Tusk refused Polish involvement outright — 'Ja się i tak na to nie zgodzę' ('I won't agree to that anyway') — noting Poland's land, air and naval forces are still being built up and its naval assets must serve Baltic security; on a possible NATO discussion of protecting the Strait of Hormuz, Foreign Minister Sikorski said Poland would consider it out of respect for its American ally, while President Nawrocki excluded Polish Armed Forces participation [31a17]. A presidential adviser publicly criticised Washington for striking without consulting allies [e1a73].

None of these is a restriction on access to Polish territory. Poland's objection ran the other way: the Irish Times reported that the US misjudgment on European bases "riled other European governments as well, notably in the Baltics and Poland" [f4b56] — Poland was displeased with the states that restricted access, not among them. The immediate pre-war baseline was routine: the US-Poland EDCA Joint Commission met on 26-27 February 2026, "reaffirming the shared commitment to enhancing U.S. readiness and the security of NATO's eastern flank", with no Iran or overflight friction recorded [9c6f7]. In parallel, general military integration deepened during the war: the US Air Force's second-largest War Reserve Materiel site in Europe was completed at Powidz, marked on 27 May [2e5f1], and on 3 June Poland formally proposed a new permanent US base [3f6a2]. Poland also backed reopening the Strait of Hormuz diplomatically [0c927].

how_to_refuse.text:
For foreign military aircraft not covered by a standing treaty exemption, the authority that grants — and can therefore withhold — permission is the Operational Commander of the Branches of the Armed Forces, who may simply refuse the zezwolenie under Border Act art. 18a(1) (the Minister of National Defence may delegate issuance) [5e2b3]. Enforcement against an unauthorized foreign military flight runs under art. 18b, not art. 18a: the state air-traffic-management organ issues the summons, and the Operational Commander decides interception and, as a last resort, destruction measures 'w formie rozkazu' (in the form of an order) [6f3c4].

Whether that permission requirement reaches US flights for this war is unresolved. Art. 18a(3)(3)(c) exempts a flight only where it is "związany z wykonywaniem zadań wynikających z umów międzynarodowych" ("connected with the performance of tasks arising from international agreements") binding on Poland, and only "jeżeli obowiązek udostępnienia przestrzeni powietrznej Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej wynika z tych umów" ("if the obligation to make available the airspace of the Republic of Poland arises from those agreements") [5e2b3] — two cumulative conditions. Nothing establishes that flights supporting operations against Iran perform tasks arising from EDCA: the government's own ratification memorandum frames the agreement solely as bilateral defence cooperation and NATO eastern-flank deterrence, without reference to airspace, to article 13, or to operations beyond that scope, and the ratification statute amended the Border Act in no respect — art. 18a having been enacted in 2001, nineteen years before EDCA [5b8c4]. No Polish parliamentary question, ministerial answer or legal commentary addressing the point was located.

refusal_history.text: No precedent of Poland refusing US military overflight, landing or basing was located, in 2026 or earlier. In the 2026 US-Israel-Iran war Poland appeared in no comparative survey of European states restricting US access [0d7a8][8b5e6], and no episode of Poland denying, revoking or suspending a US military flight was found.
