counterfactual.text: Romania is on the default and most common route. US military aircraft would need to reroute via Slovakia and Hungary to the Adriatic via Slovenia or Croatia, and from the Adriatic fly across the Mediterranean. This significantly lengthens the path. Additionally, Romanian bases could not be used for resupply. However, the use of Romanian bases is frequent. It is not likely that the Romanian government would take this action.

prose.footnote: ADS-B gaps over Romania hide crossings, so the share counted by a flight's own crossing is an undercount.

authorization_mechanism.text: US Government aircraft and civil aircraft operating under contract exclusively for the US Department of Defense hold a standing treaty authorization to overfly Romania, refuel in the air, and land and take off, granted by Article VII of the 2005 US-Romania agreement (in force since 21 July 2006, evergreen under Article XVI) [a3f2c]. That authorization is qualified: it applies 'in full compliance with the specific air-traffic-safety regulations and in accordance with the procedures agreed by the parties or the designated authorities,' and the concrete procedures live in unpublished implementing arrangements under Article XI, so whether routine per-flight diplomatic clearance is thereby eliminated cannot be confirmed from the record [a3f2c]. In parallel, Romanian aviation law conditions foreign-military overflight on an overflight approval issued by the Ministry of Transport with the binding aviz of the Ministry of National Defence [b1d4e].

cooperation_2026.text: Romania cooperated with US military operations during the 2026 Iran war. On 11 March 2026, following a meeting of Romanian defense officials in Bucharest, the United States was granted permission to use bases in NATO ally Romania for operations in Iran, a decision taken after President Nicusor Dan called a defense-council (CSAT) meeting to weigh whether to allow US aircraft to carry out such missions [d2e81]. The grant was thus case-by-case and mission-specific, exercised through the President/CSAT approval channel of the foreign-armed-forces law rather than flowing automatically [c7a90][d2e81].

how_to_refuse.text: Romania's clearest lawful refusal lever operates at the level of new operations or use of its bases and airspace for a mission: under Article 4 of Legea 291/2007 the President, on the Prime Minister's proposal and after consulting CSAT, approves — and may decline — entry, stationing, operations, or transit of foreign armed forces, a power exercised in March 2026 over the US Iran missions [c7a90][d2e81]. The Ministry of National Defence holds an additional lever through its binding overflight aviz and its air-traffic-safety authority, with notifications routed to its Overflight, Relations and Aeronautical Regulations Section [b1d4e][e5f63]. However, because routine overflight by US Government and DoD-contract aircraft is treaty-authorized under Article VII of the 2005 agreement, a blanket refusal of such routine overflight would implicate the treaty rather than be a purely discretionary domestic act; on this text, conditioning or refusing a new operation does not on its face require treaty renegotiation — an inference from the DCA's structure [a3f2c], not a stated provision.

refusal_history.text: No refusal by Romania of a US military overflight, landing, or basing request is documented in the available legal corpus; the recent record shows the opposite. In March 2026 Romania's President convened the Supreme Council of National Defence (CSAT) and the United States was granted permission to use bases in Romania for operations relating to Iran [d2e81]. Romania is a NATO ally hosting stationed US forces under the standing 2005 access agreement, which authorizes rather than bars US overflight [a3f2c].

authorization_mechanism.text: No published treaty was located that grants automatic US military overflight of Saudi Arabia: the bilateral defence relationship appears to rest on executive agreements, though the principal cited source (4b9e7, CRS RL33533) does not discuss US military overflight within its scope, so this reflects an absence of located evidence rather than a confirmed absence of any treaty [4b9e7]. Permission is per-flight sovereign clearance: the current Saudi eAIP GEN 1.2 requires all foreign diplomatic and military flight requests to be submitted via diplomatic channels to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) [a3c91]. FAA International Flight Information Manual guidance states that US requests for overflights or technical stops of aircraft carrying military personnel or supplies go through the US Embassy at least 15 days in advance, via MOFA, with Ministry of Defense (and Aviation) approval and disclosure of purpose of flight and routing [7f24b]. Military aircraft are excluded from the Civil Aviation Law's scope (Royal Decree M/44, Art. 3(4)), and the law declares the Kingdom's complete and absolute sovereignty over its airspace (Art. 2) [e58d2].

cooperation_2026.text: During the 2026 US-Iran war, Saudi Arabia was cooperating with US military air operations in a defensive/support capacity: NBC News reports the Saudis "allowed the U.S. to fly aircraft from [Prince Sultan Air Base] to support the war in Iran, as well as allowing aircraft based in nearby countries to fly over" [c1f06]. NBC News reports Saudi Arabia broadly supported US air operations from Prince Sultan Air Base and allowed overflight from nearby countries [c1f06]. The exception was the Project Freedom Hormuz operation, where Saudi Arabia suspended US access after Trump announced the operation without prior consultation (see refusal_history) [c1f06]. After the brief Project Freedom suspension, US access was restored (see refusal_history).

how_to_refuse.text: Because clearance is granted per flight, refusal requires no treaty renegotiation: the state simply withholds or revokes clearance through the MOFA diplomatic channel prescribed by eAIP GEN 1.2 [a3c91]. Military aircraft sit outside the Civil Aviation Law (Art. 3(4)), so refusal is an exercise of the executive's sovereign discretion over the Kingdom's airspace (Art. 2); GACA's permit power under Art. 9 operates within the law's scope, from which military aircraft are excluded (Art. 3(4)) [e58d2]. Under the FAA IFIM procedure, the Ministry of Defense approval step provides a distinct veto point before clearance is granted [7f24b]. In practice, denials of strategic scope are decided at Crown Prince/royal-leadership level, as with the 27 January 2026 declared policy against any airspace use for military action against Iran [92ad3] and the May 2026 mission-specific suspension of Prince Sultan Air Base use and overflight [c1f06].

refusal_history.text: On 13 April 2024, during Iran's first direct attack on Israel, Saudi Arabia (with the UAE) refused a US request to open its airspace to US and Israeli interceptor aircraft, while still sharing intelligence (WSJ-derived reporting) [b2664]. On 27 January 2026, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told Iranian President Pezeshkian, per the SPA readout, that the Kingdom "will not allow the use of its airspace or territory in any military actions against the Islamic Republic of Iran or any attacks by any party, regardless of their destination" — a standing declared-policy refusal [92ad3]. On ~3-6 May 2026, after President Trump's unconsulted announcement of the "Project Freedom" Hormuz operation, Saudi Arabia informed the US it would not allow US aircraft to fly from Prince Sultan Air Base or through Saudi airspace to support it — a mission-specific suspension decided at royal-leadership level [c1f06]. The restrictions were lifted around 7 May 2026 (WSJ, citing US and Saudi officials) after a second Trump-MbS call [5c8fa].

counterfactual.text: Currently due to Swiss, Austrian, and Italian policy, overflight of Slovenia and Croatia is near zero. However, if any of Romania, Bulgaria or Greece were to block, then the ability of US military aircraft to transit between Hungary and the Adriatic via Slovenia or Croatia would be decisive.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of Slovenia is authorized per flight, under the diplomatic-clearance regime for all foreign state aircraft [5a7d1]. Under the 2024 Aviation Act (ZLet-1) Art. 285(1), a foreign state aircraft may overfly, land, or depart only under a permit issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 'unless international treaties binding the Republic of Slovenia ... provide otherwise' [5a7d1]. The MFA issues that permit 'in agreement with' the Ministry of Defence (Art. 286(7)) [e2b48]. Permits may be single (per flight or series), annual, or permanent, and are filed electronically to the MFA (Art. 286(1)-(2)) [9c3f0]; the AIP requires the clearance to be submitted five days before entering Slovenian airspace, disclosing operator, route, purpose, and status, with an issued clearance valid for 24 hours [b71e9]. NATO membership does not displace the permit: the Art. 250(1) exception for aircraft under NATO operational command is only a weapons-carriage easement, not a standing overflight clearance [d4c76].

cooperation_2026.text: Slovenia kept its airspace open to US military aircraft during the 2026 Iran war. On 8 April 2026, asked whether it would follow neighbouring Austria in closing its airspace to American military aircraft, the Slovenian Government Communication Office (UKOM) stated on the record to Delo that 'the government has not adopted such a decision' [f5a20]. Consistently, Slovenia was not named in any 2026 round-up of European states restricting US military airspace or base access [a06f3][62d9c].

how_to_refuse.text: Slovenia can lawfully refuse specific US military flights, or a mission class, without renegotiating any treaty. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issues the required per-flight permit 'in agreement with' the Ministry of Defence (ZLet-1 Arts. 285(1), 286(7)), and the application must disclose the flight's purpose and any weapons and dangerous goods aboard (Art. 286(4)) [5a7d1][e2b48]. For armed missions the bar is firmer: carriage of usable armament, EW, or reconnaissance equipment (Art. 250) and of military weapons, ammunition, explosives, or armed foreign troops (Art. 252) is permitted only in enumerated cases or when the Government (Vlada) so decides per case on the Defence Ministry's proposal — so such a flight is barred by default absent a Government decision [d4c76][8e1b5]. The AIP states categorically that 'flights carrying munition and weapons of war will not be permitted to enter airspace of the Republic of Slovenia' [3f9a2]. A blanket closure to all US flights is legally available but would be a Government-level political act — one the Government stated in April 2026 it had not taken [f5a20].

refusal_history.text: No episode of Slovenia refusing US military overflight, landing, or basing was located in any era — across the 2026 Iran-war airspace-restriction round-ups, which name Austria, Switzerland, Italy, Spain, and France but never Slovenia [a06f3][62d9c], the 1999 Kosovo period, and the 2003 Iraq war. US Embassy Ljubljana describes the US military presence in Slovenia as the Defense Attaché Office, identifying no US base [8b98f][8fe12]. On 8 April 2026 the government stated on the record that it had taken no airspace-closure decision (see cooperation_2026) [f5a20]. The contrary record includes 1999, when Slovenia as a Partnership-for-Peace state offered NATO the use of its airspace for air strikes against the FRY [17b4e]. Because per-flight clearances are unpublished, this is 'none located,' not proof that none occurred.

counterfactual.text: Blocking Slovak airspace would severely complicate US logistics and force costly rerouting for the relevant theater. Hungary and Slovakia are in the unique position of a single point of failure: each individually connects the no-fly zone across Spain, France, Switzerland and Austria in the west, with the one across Ukraine and Russia in the east. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has sharply criticized the US War on Iran, but he and the Slovak Parliament have not used their power to take this action. Blocking Slovak airspace would block all US flights to or from the theater using British or German resupply stations, as well as direct arcs between the United States and the Middle East. Flights would need to pass without resupply across the Mediterranean south of Spain. The throughput of the US' Mediterranean bases for this volume is unverified. If the Slovak government looked likely to deny overflight, it is most likely that without wider European backing, the US would threaten them or offer concessions. However, this does put the Slovak government in a position of extraordinary leverage.

authorization_mechanism.text: US military overflight of Slovakia runs on a standing treaty right rather than per-flight clearance. Under Article 11 of the 2022 US-Slovakia Defense Cooperation Agreement (in force 1 April 2022), aircraft operated by or exclusively for US forces are authorized to over-fly, conduct aerial refuelling, land and take off within Slovak territory, may not be boarded or inspected without US consent, and are exempt from air-navigation and airport charges [a1f30]. Routine overflight is de-individualised: an annual reciprocal permission is arranged in advance rather than approving each flight separately [7b2e9]. The general regime for other foreign state aircraft — a diplomatic note with a clearance request to the MFA Diplomatic Protocol at least 3 working days ahead (10 days if weapons, ammunition, armed persons or explosives are aboard) — is retained for non-DCA flights and for US landings [c4d18][e9a52]. Slovakia keeps responsibility for airspace protection and decides which spaces US forces use [3f6b7].

cooperation_2026.text: On 3 March 2026, Defence Minister Robert Kaliňák addressed continuing US military overflights bound for the Middle East: NATO-framework military flights are subject only to notification, with permits required only for landings — 'Zakázať im to nemôžeme' ('we cannot ban them') [12bc4][f7eb1]; the government did not ban the flights even though it had condemned the attacks on Iran as contrary to international law [8c7f4]. Kaliňák stated the US aircraft involved were transport and logistics aircraft, not combat aircraft (fighters or bombers) [8c7f4]. Slovak media reported a high volume of military overflights during the war [8c7f4].

how_to_refuse.text: Several Slovak authorities can lawfully condition or refuse specific US flights without touching the treaty, though the clearest levers bite at landing and cargo rather than routine overflight. Slovakia's distinct approval is required for a DCA aircraft to land, and for any flight carrying dangerous cargo (weapons, ammunition, armed persons, explosives), which the MFA Diplomatic Protocol handles on a longer 10-day track — both are retained refusal points [c4d18][e9a52]. Under §6 of the aviation act (zákon 143/1998) the Ministry of Transport, in agreement with the Ministry of Defence, may declare flight prohibitions or restrictions over Slovak airspace [d2c84]. Constitutionally, consent to the presence of foreign armed forces on Slovak territory belongs to the National Council (čl. 86 písm. m), while the Government decides on consent to transit of foreign armed forces and to their presence for humanitarian aid, exercises or peace-observation missions (čl. 119 písm. o) [5e1a9]. DCA Article 11 grants US-forces aircraft a standing right to overfly Slovak territory [a1f30].
